newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Women barely get a look-in at APEC summit.
newsitem.headline: Women barely get a look-in at APEC summit.

text.p: Asia-Pacific leaders gathering here for their annual summit may represent half of humanity in a vast and diverse region, but women have no place at their top table.
For all their differences, leaders of the 18 economies in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum make up an exclusively male club.
The best-known female dignitary coming for the summit in Subic Bay on Monday, Hillary Clinton, plays only a supporting role as U.S. First Lady.
As is customary on such occasions, she and other wives will have their own special programme of shopping and sightseeing while their menfolk work away at changing the world.
Women's rights activists say the serried ranks of suits at APEC show that women have little political or economic clout in a region of four billion people.

"The fact that there are few (female) leaders and ministers in Asia-Pacific reflects a situation where women do not have equal participation in government. This speaks of the status of women in the region," said Liza Maza, who leads a feminist alliance against APEC's plan to create the world's biggest free trade area.

Although no women leaders will take part in the lofty summit pleasantries and photo opportunities, a handful of women tackled the nitty gritty of trade and investment liberalisation in more lowly ministerial talks.

China and the United States sent female trade negotiators. U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and China's trade minister Wu Yi met face-to-face on the major issue bedevilling relations between the American and Asian superpowers.

Malaysia's feisty trade minister, Rafidah Aziz, Hong Kong Trade and Industry Secretary Denise Yue and Thailand's deputy minister of commerce, Sukon Kanchanalai, were among other women labouring on the foothills of the summit.

One of Asia's most prominent women leaders of recent years, Imelda Marcos, wielded power through her late husband President Ferdinand Marcos. In Manila today she sits on APEC's sidelines, a congresswoman under threat of imprisonment for corruption, watching impotently as the conference proceeds in the grand centre she built.
Although Asia can boast a bevy of women ministers, they often hold "soft" portfolios like health or education.
In Japan, where scandals deter many women from entering the political arena, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new cabinet has only one woman, the environment minister.

"Historically, the Asia-Pacific region has been dominated by male leaders. Formal politics is their game. There have been a few women, such as Cory Aquino, but this is more of an accident than from their own merits," said Maza.
Former Philippine president Corazon Aquino inspired the "People's Power" movement which toppled strongman Marcos a decade ago.
But in common with other women in Asia who have risen to supreme power in their countries, her route was through family ties, as the widow of assassinated opposition leader Benigno Aquino.

Female rulers of Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka -- and the current crop of prominent dissidents in Burma and Indonesia -- all have been daughters of male leaders whose focus on power and webs of contacts enabled their children to flourish.

Their less privileged sisters working mainly in the fields or service industries face exploitation and unemployment in a free-market system, says Nanette Miranda of the Women Workers' Movement (Philippines).
"It is women who are the first to be hit by retrenchments because of the nature of their jobs," she said.

Despite being painted by leftwingers as a heartless bunch of capitalists, APEC is looking at ways of easing the pain that economic reform and free trade can bring to local industries. A business advisory council has stressed the need to give vulnerable groups, in whose impoverished and overworked ranks Asian women still figure prominently, the skills and training they need to compete when tariff barriers come down.
